questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning of Principles of Management' refers to.
questions.a: Broad and general guidelines that steer managerial decisions and conduct; unlike the laws of pure science they concern people, so they are applied with judgement rather than mechanically.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning of Principles of Management'.
questions.a: They sit apart from techniques (step-by-step procedures) and from values (moral preferences): principles guide the use of both.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning of Principles of Management' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: lebs102.txt lines 125-219 (The Concept; principles vs techniques vs values))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nature of Principles of Management' refers to.
questions.a: Seven qualities that describe these guidelines: they reach every kind of organisation, only suggest rather than prescribe, grow out of practice and experiments, bend to circumstances, chiefly address human behaviour, link causes with effects, and depend on the prevailing situation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nature of Principles of Management'.
questions.a: Pick the quality from the clue -- pay fixed by contribution and paying capacity shows the contingent quality; same rule in a firm and a government office shows universal applicability.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nature of Principles of Management' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 2.1 (source: lebs102.txt lines 220-477 (Nature: universal applicability through contingent))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Significance of Principles of Management' refers to.
questions.a: The payoffs managers gain by using the principles: sharper reading of real situations, leaner use of scarce resources and cleaner administration, fact-based decisions, readiness for a shifting environment, discharge of social duties, and a base for training, education and research.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Significance of Principles of Management'.
questions.a: Six uses to memorise -- insights into reality, optimum utilisation with effective administration, scientific decisions, meeting change, social responsibility, and management teaching plus research.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Significance of Principles of Management' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.1 (source: lebs102.txt lines 586-816 (Significance i to vi))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management' refers to.
questions.a: F.W. Taylor's prescription for replacing personal guesswork with studied method: investigate work scientifically instead of relying on rule of thumb, build complete goodwill and a changed mindset between managers and workers, prefer joint effort to individualism, and develop every employee to full capacity through scientific selection and training.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management'.
questions.a: Four principles -- science over rule of thumb, harmony over discord, cooperation over individualism, plus development of every person; the underlying demand is a mental revolution on both sides.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.1 (source: lebs102.txt lines 999-1320 (Principles of Scientific Management i to iv, mental revolution))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Functional Foremanship' refers to.
questions.a: Taylor's shop-floor arrangement that splits supervision among eight specialists: a planning wing (route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian) led by a planning incharge, and an execution wing (gang boss, speed boss, repair boss, inspector) led by a production incharge.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Functional Foremanship'.
questions.a: It extends division of work to supervision because no single person holds all the qualities of a good foreman; each worker then takes orders from eight bosses in their own spheres.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Functional Foremanship' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.1 (source: lebs102.txt lines 1331-1406 (Functional Foremanship, planning and production incharge))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Standardisation and Simplification of Work' refers to.
questions.a: Twin techniques for tidy production: standardisation fixes benchmarks for materials, tools, time, methods and conditions that all output must meet, while simplification cuts away surplus varieties, sizes and models so that fewer lines are made and stored.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Standardisation and Simplification of Work'.
questions.a: Standardisation raises quality and interchangeability; simplification trims inventory, labour and machine cost.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Standardisation and Simplification of Work' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.2 (source: lebs102.txt lines 1407-1493 (Standardisation and Simplification, objectives i to iv))

concepts.title: Work Study Techniques: Method, Motion and Fatigue

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Work Study Techniques: Method, Motion and Fatigue' refers to.
questions.a: Three of Taylor's investigation tools: method study hunts for the single best way of arranging a job, motion study strips out unproductive body movements, and fatigue study fixes how often and how long rest intervals should be.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Work Study Techniques: Method, Motion and Fatigue'.
questions.a: Method study covers the whole flow from raw material to delivery; motion study classifies movements as productive, incidental or unproductive; fatigue study guards stamina and output.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Work Study Techniques: Method, Motion and Fatigue' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.3 (source: lebs102.txt lines 1494-1613 (Method Study, Motion Study, Fatigue Study))

concepts.title: Time Study and the Standard Task

questions.q: Using the method 'Time Study and the Standard Task', work with: minutes_per_hour = 240, minutes_per_unit = 5, rest_hours = 25, shift_hours = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of units_per_shift.
questions.a: 13200 rupees

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Time Study and the Standard Task' and work with: minutes_per_hour = 10, minutes_per_unit = 20, rest_hours = 50, shift_hours = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of units_per_shift.
questions.a: 0 rupees

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Time Study and the Standard Task' refers to.
questions.a: Time study measures with devices how long each element of a job should take, and from several readings fixes a standard time; that standard then converts into the number of units a worker must finish in a shift.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Time Study and the Standard Task'.
questions.a: The standard task decided by time study anchors worker numbers, incentive schemes and labour cost.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Time Study and the Standard Task', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: units_per_shift = (shift_hours - rest_hours) * minutes_per_hour / minutes_per_unit

questions.q: Using the method 'Differential Piece Wage System', work with: rate_per_unit = 25, units_produced = 12. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of daily_wage.
questions.a: 300 years

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Differential Piece Wage System' and work with: rate_per_unit = 100, units_produced = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of daily_wage.
questions.a: 500 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Differential Piece Wage System' refers to.
questions.a: Taylor's pay scheme that separates efficient from inefficient workers: those reaching or beating the standard output earn a higher rate per piece, those below it earn a lower rate, so the wage gap itself motivates better performance.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Differential Piece Wage System'.
questions.a: One output standard, two rates -- above or at standard gets the higher rate, below it the lower; the reward difference pushes output up.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Differential Piece Wage System', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: daily_wage = units_produced * rate_per_unit

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fayol's Fourteen Principles of Management' refers to.
questions.a: Henri Fayol's general rules for running any organisation, drawn from his own managing experience: division of work, discipline, unity of command, authority matched with responsibility, unity of direction, fair pay, scalar chain, order, equity, stable tenure, initiative, team spirit, a balance of centralisation and decentralisation, and the organisation's interest placed above any single person's.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fayol's Fourteen Principles of Management'.
questions.a: In case questions, name the principle breached -- an order placed with a relative breaches the rule that the organisation's interest outranks any individual's; confusion from two bosses breaches unity of command.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Fayol's Fourteen Principles of Management' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.1 (source: lebs102.txt lines 1897-2554 (The 14 principles i to xiv))

concepts.title: Unity of Command versus Unity of Direction

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Unity of Command versus Unity of Direction' refers to.
questions.a: Two distinct Fayol principles: unity of command insists each employee answers to exactly one boss to prevent dual subordination, while unity of direction requires that all activities chasing the same objective share one head and one plan to stop overlapping effort.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Unity of Command versus Unity of Direction'.
questions.a: Command concerns a single employee's reporting line; direction concerns a whole group of activities with one goal -- individual versus organisation-wide reach.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Unity of Command versus Unity of Direction' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.2 (source: lebs102.txt lines 2040-2101 (Unity of Command, Unity of Direction) and the comparison table at lines 2150-2173)

concepts.title: Scalar Chain and the Gang Plank

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Scalar Chain and the Gang Plank' refers to.
questions.a: The formal ladder of authority and communication running from the highest to the lowest rank, which messages normally must climb rung by rung; in an emergency Fayol permits a same-level shortcut, the gang plank, so urgent talks are not delayed.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Scalar Chain and the Gang Plank'.
questions.a: The chain keeps order; the gang plank is the sanctioned exception for emergencies -- not a licence to bypass hierarchy routinely.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Scalar Chain and the Gang Plank' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.3 (source: lebs102.txt lines 2255-2322 (Scalar Chain, E-to-O example, Gang Plank))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fayol versus Taylor -- a Comparison' refers to.
questions.a: The two classical thinkers differ in vantage point and purpose: Fayol wrote from the top-management seat about overall administration and offered universally applicable principles from personal experience, while Taylor wrote from the shop floor about raising productivity through observation and experiment for specialised industrial situations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fayol versus Taylor -- a Comparison'.
questions.a: Remember the pairs -- top level versus shop floor, universal versus specialised, experience versus experimentation, administration versus productivity, practitioner versus scientist; their contributions still complement each other.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Fayol versus Taylor -- a Comparison' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.1 (source: lebs102.txt lines 2572-2639 (Fayol Versus Taylor comparison table))
